strengths: Addresses an important problem: directly optimizing empirical 0–1 loss for interpretable linear classifiers.
Combines geometric enumeration with sensible upper-bound pruning and provides detailed algorithm listings.
Reports improvements over common surrogate-loss baselines on small UCI datasets, alongside synthetic timing and pruning studies.
weaknesses: The central correctness proof contains an invalid inference. Appendix A assumes that greater Hamming distance from an optimal cell's predictions implies greater loss against the true labels; optimality does not imply this ordering. Moreover, Equation (2) counts zero predictions as errors, whereas loss01 treats them as correct. The proof needs an explicit, justified construction connecting boundary assignments to an actual classifier achieving the claimed loss.

The displayed implementation violates exactness even on data in general position. In one dimension, points (1, 1+1e-9, 1+2e-9) with labels (+1, -1, +1) require at least one classification error. However, the 1e-8 threshold makes all predictions zero for the enumerated boundaries, and loss01 reports zero errors. This is a concrete failure of the advertised exactness guarantee.

The stated assumptions do not ensure that fitw is defined. The noncollinear points (1,1), (2,2), and (1,2) satisfy Definition 1, yet selecting the first two produces a singular linear system; rotatePivot has no termination condition for this case. Handling of repeated or coplanar observations is also absent, limiting applicability to datasets with discrete features.

The novelty claim is insufficiently established against classical hyperplane-arrangement enumeration and Nguyen and Sanner (2013), whose similar polynomial combinatorial algorithm is explicitly acknowledged. The manuscript does not convincingly establish what substantial algorithmic advance, beyond the proposed derivation and pruning, supports its claim of solving a longstanding open problem.

The evaluation lacks comparisons with existing exact MIP or branch-and-bound methods, independent checks of optimality, and comparative runtime or memory measurements. Five datasets with at most six features cannot establish broad practicality. Hardware, preprocessing, baseline tuning, and the experimental C++ implementation and maximum-margin reconstruction are insufficiently documented.

The generalization claims exceed both theory and evidence. Equation (1) supplies an upper bound; minimizing its empirical-loss term does not guarantee optimal or uniformly superior test accuracy. Table 2 includes ties and substantial fold variability, without statistical evidence supporting the abstract's claim of optimal out-of-sample accuracy.
